title: Spoke-type ferrite rotor with flux concentration

ideaData.title: Spoke-type ferrite rotor with flux concentration
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 8; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R5
ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor permanent magnets; Rotor core lamination stack; Stator hairpin winding
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Interior permanent magnet rotor with sintered NdFeB buried in flux barriers. Proposal: Ferrite magnets arranged radially in a spoke layout so the pole area concentrates flux from a larger magnet cross-section. Flux concentration compensates for ferrite's lower remanence, roughly 0.4 T against 1.2 T for NdFeB. Published cost work puts ferrite at a tenth to a twentieth of rare earth magnet cost per kg.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Ferrite runs at roughly 5-10% of sintered NdFeB per kg. Even at three times the magnet volume the material cost falls sharply, though rotor and stator both grow.
ideaData.riskNotes: Ferrite demagnetises at LOW temperature, the opposite of NdFeB, so the cold-start demagnetisation case governs and must be tested at minus 40 degrees. Rotor mechanical design is harder because spoke geometry weakens the lamination bridges at 16,000 rpm. The machine grows for equal torque.
ideaData.validationRequired: Cold demagnetisation testing at minus 40 degrees with peak current, rotor burst test at 1.2 times maximum speed given the weakened bridges, and full torque-speed mapping.
ideaData.investmentText: High. New rotor and stator tooling, full electromagnetic redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No volume production benchmark in a premium BEV. Ferrite spoke rotors are at supplier demonstrator stage
ideaData.practiceNote: No volume production benchmark in a premium BEV; ferrite spoke rotors are in laboratory and supplier demonstrator stage

title: Switched reluctance machine with no magnets and no rotor winding

ideaData.title: Switched reluctance machine with no magnets and no rotor winding
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 9; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R5
ideaData.targetFunctions: Generate Flux; Sustain Field; Switch Current
ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor permanent magnets; Rotor core lamination stack; Power module (SiC)
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Interior permanent magnet machine with sintered NdFeB. Proposal: A salient laminated rotor with no magnets, no windings and no electrical connections at all. The rotor becomes a simple stamped and stacked steel part. Published comparisons put the machine cost reduction at 40-60% while accepting roughly 85-90% efficiency against 95% or better for an IPM.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The rotor becomes a bare laminated steel stack with no magnets, no copper and no assembly beyond stacking. This is the cheapest rotor that can be built.
ideaData.riskNotes: Torque ripple and acoustic noise are the historic barriers and both are severe on a premium application. Requires a bespoke converter topology and high-bandwidth control, so inverter cost and complexity rise. The efficiency penalty is a range penalty the customer pays for.
ideaData.validationRequired: Acoustic and torque ripple measurement against the premium NVH target, converter topology development, and efficiency mapping to quantify the range penalty.
ideaData.investmentText: High. New machine, new converter topology, new control software.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No mainstream passenger BEV in volume production. Developed by Enedym and others for cost-sensitive segments
ideaData.practiceNote: No mainstream passenger BEV in volume production; developed by Enedym and others for cost-sensitive segments

title: Axial flux machine in place of radial flux

ideaData.title: Axial flux machine in place of radial flux
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 10; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R5
ideaData.targetFunctions: Generate Flux; Transmit Torque; Enclose Components
ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor permanent magnets; Rotor core lamination stack; Stator core lamination stack; Main housing
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Radial flux interior permanent magnet machine with a long axial stack. Proposal: An axial flux topology places the flux path along the axis, giving a short large-diameter pancake machine. Torque density is higher, so for equal torque the active material volume falls, taking magnet, copper and steel with it. Packaging changes completely and the housing shortens.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Higher torque density means less active material for equal output. Magnet, copper and electrical steel all scale down together, which is why the saving is broad rather than concentrated.
ideaData.riskNotes: Axial rotor attraction forces are large and must be reacted by a stiff structure, which adds back some mass and cost. Manufacturing maturity is far lower and the supply base is narrow. Packaging change is total, so this is a programme-start decision only.
ideaData.validationRequired: Structural analysis of axial attraction forces, full torque-speed and thermal mapping, and manufacturing capability audit of the limited supply base.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Entirely new machine and packaging, new supply base.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Mercedes-AMG models using YASA axial flux machines. YASA has announced rare-earth-free axial flux development
ideaData.practiceNote: Mercedes-AMG models using YASA axial flux machines; YASA is developing rare-earth-free variants

title: Iron nitride or other rare-earth-free magnet chemistry

ideaData.title: Iron nitride or other rare-earth-free magnet chemistry
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 11; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Technology not production ready within programme timing
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Sintered NdFeB with heavy rare earth addition. Proposal: Iron nitride magnet chemistry uses no rare earth elements at all. Development is funded and backed by major OEM investment, but it is not in volume automotive production and energy product is currently below sintered NdFeB, so more volume is needed for equal flux.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removes rare earth content entirely, so both the material cost and the price volatility exposure disappear. The offset is more magnet volume for equal flux.
ideaData.riskNotes: Not production-ready. Energy product is below NdFeB so the rotor must be redesigned around more magnet volume. Treat this as a technology to track and second-source against, not a current programme option. Committing to it now is a schedule risk.
ideaData.validationRequired: Magnetic characterisation against the demagnetisation envelope, thermal stability over service life, and supply capacity confirmation before any commitment.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Technology watch now, redesign if it matures.
ideaData.timeToImplement: Beyond current programme timing. Track, do not commit.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Not in production. Niron Magnetics iron nitride chemistry, with Stellantis and GM investment, announced for future Chrysler and Jeep applications

title: Permanent magnet assisted synchronous reluctance with reduced magnet volume

ideaData.title: Permanent magnet assisted synchronous reluctance with reduced magnet volume
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 12; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R5
ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor permanent magnets; Rotor core lamination stack
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Interior permanent magnet rotor where magnet torque dominates. Proposal: Shift the torque split toward reluctance and use the magnets only to raise power factor and cut stator ohmic loss. Magnet volume falls substantially while efficiency stays close to a full IPM, because reluctance torque does the work. This is the least disruptive of the magnet-reduction routes.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Magnet volume falls by roughly a third to a half while the machine keeps most of its efficiency, because reluctance torque substitutes for magnet torque rather than being lost.
ideaData.riskNotes: Requires a multi-barrier rotor design and a control strategy tuned to the reluctance torque, so maximum torque per amp control becomes more complex. Torque ripple rises with barrier count and must be managed by skew or microgeometry. Machine may grow slightly.
ideaData.validationRequired: Torque-speed and efficiency mapping against target, torque ripple and NVH measurement, and demagnetisation check at the reduced magnet volume.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Rotor redesign and control software development.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Tesla Model 3 Long Range rear drive unit — PM-assisted synchronous reluctance machine
ideaData.practiceNote: Tesla Model 3 Long Range rear drive unit uses a PM-assisted synchronous reluctance machine

title: 400 V architecture in place of 800 V

ideaData.title: 400 V architecture in place of 800 V
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 13; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative P1
ideaData.targetFunctions: Switch Current; Conduct Current; Insulate Voltage
ideaData.componentsAffected: Power module (SiC); DC-link capacitor; AC busbar set; DC busbar; HV DC input connector
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: 800 V bus with silicon carbide devices and 800 V rated passives throughout. Proposal: A 400 V bus permits silicon IGBTs, lower-rated capacitors, connectors and insulation systems throughout. Component cost falls across the whole HV chain, not just the switch. The penalty is charging rate and cable current, which are vehicle-level attributes.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Voltage rating drives cost across every HV component simultaneously. Devices, capacitors, connectors and insulation all step down a class together, which is why the saving is broad.
ideaData.riskNotes: Charging rate is a headline product attribute on a premium SUV and 800 V is the reason it is competitive. Cable and busbar current double for the same power, so conductor cross-section grows. This is a vehicle architecture decision that sits far above the EDU.
ideaData.validationRequired: Vehicle-level charging performance simulation, thermal analysis at doubled conductor current, and full HV chain respecification.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Vehicle architecture decision, not an EDU change.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: 400 V with Si IGBT: Nissan Leaf. 800 V with SiC: Porsche Taycan, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV6, Lucid Air, Audi e-tron GT
ideaData.practiceNote: Nissan Leaf and most earlier 400 V BEVs use Si IGBT at 400 V; Porsche Taycan, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV6 and Lucid Air use 800 V with SiC

title: Full immersion oil cooling of the stator in place of a water jacket

ideaData.title: Full immersion oil cooling of the stator in place of a water jacket
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 14; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative T3
ideaData.componentsAffected: Stator hairpin winding; Stator insulation system; Coolant jacket fittings and hoses
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Water-glycol jacket around the stator with indirect cooling through the housing. Proposal: Immersing the stator directly in dielectric oil removes the thermal resistance of the housing wall and the jacket entirely. Higher current density for the same temperature rise allows a shorter stack, so the saving lands in the active materials.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removing the housing wall from the thermal path allows meaningfully higher current density, which shortens the stack and takes steel, copper and magnet volume with it.
ideaData.riskNotes: Churning and windage losses rise, offsetting some efficiency gain. The oil must be dielectric, which voids the cheaper fluid options in T3 and M8. Insulation system compatibility with continuous oil contact must be proven over the full life.
ideaData.validationRequired: Continuous power thermal testing at the worst duty, insulation compatibility with the oil over service life, and churning loss measurement across the speed range.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Cooling architecture and stator redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Nissan Ariya (internal oil dripping with axial rotor spray), Tesla Model 3 and Lucid Air — direct oil cooling

title: Delete the mechanical differential and use torque vectoring by dual motors

ideaData.title: Delete the mechanical differential and use torque vectoring by dual motors
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 15; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Stated as cost-negative at system level
ideaData.targetFunctions: Split Torque; Permit Slip; Connect Driveline
ideaData.componentsAffected: Differential case; Differential gears and cross pin; Output shafts (pair)
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Single motor with a mechanical open differential splitting torque to both wheels. Proposal: Two smaller motors, one per wheel, remove the differential entirely and give true torque vectoring. Whether this saves money depends on whether two half-size motors and two inverters cost less than one large one plus a differential, which at premium power levels they usually do not.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The differential case, its gears and its bearings are removed entirely, but a second machine and inverter are added. The net is almost certainly negative on cost and positive on capability.
ideaData.riskNotes: This almost certainly increases total EDU cost, because a second inverter and a second machine are expensive. It is in the register because it deletes the differential functions completely and because torque vectoring is a premium product attribute worth paying for. Judge as a product decision, not a cost one.
ideaData.validationRequired: Full vehicle dynamics assessment, cost comparison at system level including the second inverter, and packaging feasibility.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Complete architecture change.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Dual-motor torque vectoring without a mechanical differential: Audi e-tron S and Rimac Nevera
ideaData.practiceNote: Dual-motor torque vectoring is used across premium performance BEVs including Rimac and Audi e-tron S applications

title: Delete the electric oil pump and revert to splash and scoop lubrication

ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 16; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Motor-driven gerotor pump with on-demand flow control. Proposal: A gear-driven scoop and splash system lubricates the gear train and feeds a rotor cooling gallery passively. Removes the pump, its motor, its driver and its control software.

title: Optimise case depth to the calculated contact stress

ideaData.componentsAffected: Input pinion shaft; Intermediate helical gear; Final drive ring gear
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Uniform conservative case depth carried across all gears in the set. Proposal: Carburising time scales roughly with the square of case depth, so trimming depth to the calculated requirement per gear cuts furnace hours sharply. The lightly loaded mesh does not need the depth the heavily loaded one does.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Furnace time is the dominant cost in carburising. A 20% case depth reduction can cut cycle time by roughly a third, raising furnace throughput proportionally.
ideaData.riskNotes: Case depth is the primary defence against subsurface contact fatigue, which fails without warning late in life. Requires accurate contact stress calculation and a durability programme long enough to expose subsurface initiation.
ideaData.validationRequired: Contact fatigue durability testing to the required life, case depth and hardness profile metallurgy, and residual stress measurement.
ideaData.investmentText: Low to medium. Heat treatment recipe change and validation.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Full tooth shot peening after heat treatment. Proposal: Bending fatigue initiates at the root fillet, so peening compressive residual stress is only needed there. Masking or targeted peening cuts cycle time and media consumption, and leaves the flank surface finish undisturbed.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Gravity or low-pressure cast AlSi7Mg with substantial machining stock. Proposal: HPDC in AlSi10MnMg gives thinner walls, net-shape ribs and bosses, and far less machining allowance. Mass falls with the wall thickness.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Wall thickness falls from roughly 6-8 mm to 3-4 mm, cutting alloy mass by a quarter or more, and net-shape features remove most machining stock.
ideaData.riskNotes: HPDC porosity limits weldability and heat treatment, and any pressure-tight region needs vacuum assist or a lost core. Tooling NRE is high and needs volume to amortise. Not suitable if the housing is a structural member carrying suspension load.
ideaData.validationRequired: Casting porosity mapping, leak test on all fluid galleries, and structural fatigue test at the mounting interfaces. Weldability and heat treatment options are lost, so joint design must be reviewed.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Large HPDC tool and press capacity; needs volume to amortise.

ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 68; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative M6
ideaData.componentsAffected: Power module baseplate / pin-fin cooler; Thermal interface material
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Module baseplate bolted to a cold plate through a gap-filler thermal interface material. Proposal: A pin-fin baseplate sitting directly in the coolant stream removes the thermal interface layer and one conduction interface entirely. Junction to coolant thermal resistance falls, which then feeds the die area reduction in P2.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The thermal interface layer and one conduction interface are removed, cutting junction-to-coolant thermal resistance by roughly 20-30%, which then enables the die area reduction in P2.
ideaData.riskNotes: Coolant now contacts the module directly, so sealing and corrosion compatibility become critical and a leak is catastrophic rather than inconvenient. Coolant quality control becomes a service requirement.
ideaData.validationRequired: Junction temperature measurement at peak power, coolant-side sealing integrity and burst test, and long-term corrosion compatibility between the baseplate and coolant chemistry.
ideaData.investmentText: Medium to high. Module and housing redesign, plus coolant specification control.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Widely used across current traction inverters including Tesla Model 3 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 — direct-cooled pin-fin power modules
ideaData.practiceNote: Widely used in current traction inverters

title: Soft magnetic composite for the rotor pole pieces

ideaData.title: Soft magnetic composite for the rotor pole pieces
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 70; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative S1
ideaData.componentsAffected: Stator core lamination stack; Rotor core lamination stack
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Laminated non-oriented electrical steel throughout stator and rotor. Proposal: Soft magnetic composite is an iron powder with an insulating coating, pressed to net shape. It permits three-dimensional flux paths and removes stamping and stacking entirely for suitable geometries. Permeability is lower than laminated steel, so it suits pole pieces rather than the main flux path.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Stamping, stacking and joining are all replaced by a single pressing operation to net shape, which removes both scrap and assembly content.
ideaData.riskNotes: Saturation flux density and permeability are both below laminated steel, so the magnetic design must accommodate it or torque falls. Mechanical strength is lower, which matters on a rotating part at 16,000 rpm. Best suited to axial flux or claw-pole geometries.
ideaData.validationRequired: Magnetic characterisation against the design flux density, mechanical strength and burst testing at maximum speed, and iron loss measurement.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Powder tooling and a magnetic redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — material grade is not disclosed by OEMs
ideaData.practiceNote: No mainstream BEV traction benchmark; used in smaller machines and under development for axial flux

title: Simplify the magnet corrosion coating specification

ideaData.title: Simplify the magnet corrosion coating specification
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 72; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Nickel-copper-nickel triple-layer electroplated coating on every magnet. Proposal: Inside a sealed oil-filled rotor the magnet never sees humidity or salt. A single-layer coating, an epoxy or parylene coating, or in some cases a bare magnet is sufficient. Triple-layer nickel plating is specified out of habit from open-environment applications.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Electroplating is a multi-stage wet process on every magnet piece. Removing layers cuts process stages proportionally on a high piece-count part.
ideaData.riskNotes: Depends entirely on the rotor being genuinely sealed and staying sealed for the service life. If oil ingress carries moisture or the unit is ever opened in service, corrosion attacks the magnet directly and the failure is not recoverable.
ideaData.validationRequired: Salt spray and humidity testing at the assembly level rather than the part level, plus oil compatibility and long-term corrosion assessment.
ideaData.investmentText: Low. Coating specification change at the supplier.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — material grade is not disclosed by OEMs
ideaData.practiceNote: Coating specification is not publicly disclosed by OEMs; practice varies across suppliers

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Aramid paper slot liner specified for thermal class and mechanical robustness. title: Copper-clad aluminium busbar

ideaData.title: Copper-clad aluminium busbar
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 74; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative S7
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Solid copper busbar with plated joint faces. Proposal: An aluminium core with a metallurgically bonded copper skin gives copper joint behaviour at the terminals while the bulk conductor is aluminium. title: Polypropylene film gauge optimisation in the DC-link capacitor

ideaData.title: Polypropylene film gauge optimisation in the DC-link capacitor
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 75; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Conservative film thickness selected for maximum voltage derating. Proposal: Film capacitor cost scales with film area and therefore with thickness for a given capacitance. Trimming the derating factor toward the real bus voltage and ripple duty reduces film volume directly. Metallised polypropylene is self-healing, which is what allows the derating to be revisited.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Film area scales roughly with capacitance times derating. A 15% derating reduction cuts film volume by a similar proportion on the dominant cost element in the capacitor.
ideaData.riskNotes: Voltage derating is what buys capacitor life, and life reduction shows up as a warranty exposure years later rather than at validation. Self-healing consumes capacitance over life, so end-of-life capacitance must still meet the bus stability requirement.
ideaData.validationRequired: Accelerated life testing at maximum bus voltage and ripple, end-of-life capacitance measurement, and self-healing behaviour characterisation.
ideaData.investmentText: Low. Capacitor respecification with the supplier.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — material grade is not disclosed by OEMs
ideaData.practiceNote: Capacitor specification is not publicly disclosed; derating practice varies widely across inverter suppliers

title: Group III base oil in place of a fully synthetic polyalphaolefin

ideaData.title: Group III base oil in place of a fully synthetic polyalphaolefin
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 78; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative T3
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Fully synthetic polyalphaolefin base with a dedicated additive package. Proposal: Group III hydrocracked base oil delivers most of the viscosity index and oxidation stability of a polyalphaolefin at materially lower cost per litre. On a sealed lifetime fill of several litres this is a direct material saving.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Group III base oil runs well below polyalphaolefin per litre. On a multi-litre lifetime fill across the whole production volume this is meaningful material cost.
ideaData.riskNotes: Low-temperature viscosity is poorer, which matters for cold-start churning loss and pump pick-up at minus 30 degrees. Oxidation stability over a lifetime fill with no change interval is the real question and needs long-duration testing.

title: Transfer noise control to the vehicle audio system by active cancellation

ideaData.title: Transfer noise control to the vehicle audio system by active cancellation
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 84; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative V2
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Passive acoustic cover plus tuned hydraulic isolators absorbing noise after it is generated. Proposal: The EDU produces highly deterministic tonal noise: gear mesh orders and inverter switching orders, both of which are exactly known from rotor position and switching frequency. That is the ideal signal for active cancellation, far easier than broadband road noise. The vehicle already has speakers, amplifiers, microphones and a DSP. Feed the EDU order content into the existing road-noise cancellation system and delete the passive hardware.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The saving is a pure function transfer: the cost moves to hardware the vehicle already has and has already paid for. Marginal cost of adding EDU orders to an existing DSP is close to zero.
ideaData.riskNotes: Cancellation works at the occupant's ear, not at the source, so pass-by noise homologation is unaffected and the cover may still be needed for that. Effective only inside the cabin and only in the seats the system is tuned for. If the audio system fails the noise returns, which is a quality perception issue rather than a safety one.
ideaData.validationRequired: Cabin noise measurement with cancellation active and inactive, pass-by noise homologation confirmation, and subjective assessment across all seating positions.
ideaData.investmentText: Low in hardware, medium in software and calibration.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: See practice note — no direct production pairing for EDU-order cancellation
ideaData.practiceNote: Active road noise cancellation is in production across premium vehicles; applying it specifically to EDU order content is not a documented production practice

title: Two-phase immersion or vapour chamber cooling of the power stage

ideaData.title: Two-phase immersion or vapour chamber cooling of the power stage
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 87; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Outside programme timing — technology watch only
ideaData.targetFunctions: Dissipate Heat; Transfer Heat; Circulate Coolant
ideaData.componentsAffected: Power module (SiC); Power module baseplate / pin-fin cooler; Coolant jacket fittings and hoses
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Single-phase liquid cooling through a pin-fin baseplate in a coolant stream. Proposal: Two-phase cooling exploits latent heat rather than sensible heat, giving far higher heat flux capability at a lower temperature difference. Data centre practice has moved this way rapidly. Better cooling permits smaller SiC die area, which is the expensive element, so the saving lands in the semiconductor.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: SiC die cost scales with area, and area is set by the thermal path. A step change in cooling capability translates almost directly into die area and therefore module cost.
ideaData.riskNotes: Automotive orientation, vibration and altitude variation all disturb two-phase behaviour in ways a data centre never sees. Containment of the working fluid over fifteen years is unproven. Servicing a sealed two-phase system is not possible.
ideaData.validationRequired: Thermal performance across orientation, vibration and altitude, working fluid containment over service life, and freeze-thaw behaviour.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Fundamental cooling redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No automotive benchmark — established in data centre cooling

title: Gallium nitride devices in place of silicon carbide

ideaData.title: Gallium nitride devices in place of silicon carbide
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 88; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Outside programme timing — technology watch only
ideaData.targetFunctions: Switch Current; Block Voltage; Store Energy
ideaData.componentsAffected: Power module (SiC); DC-link capacitor; EMC filter and Y-capacitors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Silicon carbide MOSFETs switching at conventional traction frequencies. Proposal: GaN switches faster than SiC with lower switching loss, which allows a much higher switching frequency. Everything that scales inversely with frequency then shrinks: the DC-link capacitor, the EMC filter magnetics and the current ripple. The saving is in the passives, not the switch.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Passive component size scales inversely with switching frequency. Doubling frequency can roughly halve the DC-link capacitance requirement and shrink the filter magnetics proportionally.
ideaData.riskNotes: GaN device voltage ratings and automotive qualification at 800 V remain limited, and the technology is not mature for traction current levels. Very fast switching worsens EMC and puts severe stress on motor winding insulation, which may force back the insulation cost saved elsewhere.
ideaData.validationRequired: Device availability and automotive qualification at 800 V and traction current, EMC measurement at the raised switching rate, and winding insulation stress testing.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Technology watch; not currently viable at this rating.
ideaData.timeToImplement: Beyond current programme. Track device maturity.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No traction benchmark at this power and voltage — GaN established in consumer and low-power automotive

title: Phase change material thermal buffer sized for peak duty

ideaData.title: Phase change material thermal buffer sized for peak duty
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 91; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Weighted score below the 3.00 threshold
ideaData.componentsAffected: Power module (SiC); Oil-water heat exchanger; Electric oil pump
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Cooling system sized continuously for the worst-case peak thermal event. Proposal: Peak thermal events on a road vehicle are short: an overtake, a gradient, a launch. A phase change material absorbs that energy in its latent heat and releases it slowly afterwards. The cooling system can then be sized for average duty rather than peak, which is a much smaller system.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cooling hardware is sized by peak duty. Buffering the peak allows the exchanger, pump and coolant flow to be sized to the average, which is a much smaller and cheaper system.
ideaData.riskNotes: Fails exactly where it is most needed, which is sustained duty such as towing on a long gradient, because the buffer saturates and does not recover. Adds mass and volume. Once saturated the vehicle derates, which on a premium SUV is a serious attribute failure.
ideaData.validationRequired: Duty cycle analysis to confirm peaks are genuinely short, sustained tow and gradient testing to saturation, and buffer recovery rate measurement.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Thermal system redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No automotive benchmark — used in electronics and building thermal management
ideaData.practiceNote: Used in electronics and building thermal management; no automotive traction benchmark

title: Carbon fibre rotor sleeve permitting a lighter and simpler rotor structure

ideaData.title: Carbon fibre rotor sleeve permitting a lighter and simpler rotor structure
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 94; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R16
ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor shaft; Rotor core lamination stack; Rotor end plates and balance rings
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Steel lamination bridges sized to retain magnets against centrifugal load at maximum speed. Proposal: A carbon fibre containment sleeve carries the centrifugal load instead of the lamination bridges. The bridges can then be thinned or removed, which cuts magnetic flux leakage substantially and lets the same torque be produced with less magnet. The magnet saving pays for the sleeve.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Removing or thinning the bridges cuts flux leakage, so the same airgap flux needs less magnet volume. The saving is in the magnet, offset by the sleeve cost and the larger effective air gap.
ideaData.riskNotes: Carbon sleeve cost is significant and it increases the effective magnetic air gap, which works against the flux gain. Thermal expansion mismatch between carbon and steel must be managed across the temperature range. Established at very high speeds where there is no alternative, less obviously justified at 16,000 rpm.
ideaData.validationRequired: Rotor burst test at 1.2 times maximum speed, thermal cycling of the carbon-to-steel interface, and magnetic measurement to confirm the flux leakage gain.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Rotor redesign and sleeve process qualification.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Motorsport and aerospace high-speed machines; not standard in passenger BEV rotors
ideaData.practiceNote: Carbon sleeves are established in high-speed machines including motorsport and aerospace; not standard in passenger BEV traction rotors

title: Sell EDU waste heat to the cabin and battery as a designed output

ideaData.title: Sell EDU waste heat to the cabin and battery as a designed output
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 95; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative T6
ideaData.componentsAffected: Oil-water heat exchanger; Coolant jacket fittings and hoses; Electric oil pump
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: EDU heat treated purely as a loss to be rejected, with a dedicated cooling path sized to dump it. Proposal: An EDU rejects tens of kilowatts of heat. In cold weather the vehicle simultaneously spends battery energy running a heat pump for the cabin and to warm the pack for charging. Reframe the thermal system so EDU heat is a deliberate product: raise the coolant target temperature, route it to the cabin and pack first, and downsize the heat pump accordingly. The EDU cooling system stops being pure cost and starts offsetting a more expensive component.

ideaData.investmentText: High. Vehicle thermal architecture change with a cross-system owner.

title: Dry-running gear train on sealed-for-life grease and solid lubricant coatings

ideaData.title: Dry-running gear train on sealed-for-life grease and solid lubricant coatings
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 98; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Wet sump with circulating oil, pump, filter, breather and dynamic shaft seals. Proposal: Delete the oil system entirely. Grease-packed bearings, a solid lubricant coating on the gear flanks such as a tungsten carbide carbon or molybdenum disulphide layer, and no sump. Removes the oil, the pump, the filter, the breather, the baffle and the dynamic seals in one move, and the static seals become far simpler because there is no fluid to retain.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Five components and their assembly operations are removed together, along with the fill operation and the leak test that goes with a wet system.
ideaData.riskNotes: Almost certainly fails on gear durability and heat removal at premium torque. Oil does three jobs here: lubricates, cools and flushes debris, and only the first has a dry substitute. Realistically applicable to a low-torque secondary drive, not a 450 Nm primary. It is in the register because deleting five components at once deserves to be tested rather than assumed impossible.
ideaData.validationRequired: Gear scuffing and pitting durability at peak torque without oil film, bearing temperature at continuous duty, and coating wear life over the service life.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Coating process development and a full durability programme.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Single-speed reduction with the machine sized for both launch torque and top speed. Proposal: This deliberately adds cost to the gearbox to remove more from the machine. A single-speed EDU sizes the motor for peak launch torque and then wastes that capability at cruise. Two ratios let a materially smaller machine cover the same envelope, and magnet volume scales with machine size. The counter-intuitive move is spending on gears to save on rare earth.

ideaData.riskNotes: Adds a shift element, its actuator, its control software and a shift quality problem that does not currently exist. Shift shock on a premium vehicle is a refinement risk. Whether the machine saving exceeds the gearbox addition depends entirely on the magnet price, which is exactly the number this study has not validated.
ideaData.validationRequired: System trade study of machine downsizing against added gearbox content, shift quality assessment, and efficiency mapping across the cycle.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Gearbox redesign and machine resize together.

title: Delete the reduction gearbox with a direct-drive high-pole-count machine

ideaData.title: Delete the reduction gearbox with a direct-drive high-pole-count machine

ideaData.targetFunctions: Multiply Torque; Split Torque; Transmit Torque; Permit Slip
ideaData.componentsAffected: Input pinion shaft; Intermediate gear shaft; Intermediate helical gear; Final drive ring gear; Differential case; Differential gears and cross pin
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Two-stage reduction of roughly 10:1 between motor and wheels. Proposal: Invert the usual assumption. A high-pole-count machine turning at wheel speed removes the entire gear train, its bearings, its oil system and its NVH content. The machine becomes large in diameter and torque dense rather than fast and small, which suits an axial flux topology.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The entire gear train, its bearings and its lubrication system are removed. The offset is a much larger machine, which is why the net is probably negative.
ideaData.riskNotes: The machine grows enormously because torque scales with volume and there is no ratio multiplying it. Magnet and copper content rise far more than the gearbox saving, so at premium torque this is very likely cost-negative overall. It is here because it eliminates six components and an entire function branch, and because axial flux changes the arithmetic enough to be worth checking rather than dismissing.
ideaData.validationRequired: Machine sizing study at wheel-speed torque, packaging feasibility within the axle envelope, and unsprung or sprung mass assessment.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Complete architecture change.
ideaData.timeToImplement: Beyond current programme. Likely cost-negative; test the arithmetic.

ideaData.title: Buy magnet function rather than magnets, with supplier ownership and end-of-life take-back
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 101; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Displaced by higher scoring alternative R19
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Magnets purchased outright at a fixed annual price, with no residual value recovered at end of life. Proposal: Contract for magnetic performance over the vehicle life rather than for a physical part, with the supplier retaining title and an obligation to recover the material at end of life. The recovered rare earth has real value, so the supplier can price the initial supply below outright purchase. This attacks the single largest line in the bill of materials through the contract rather than the design.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Recovered magnet material retains substantial value. Sharing that residual with the supplier lets the initial price fall without the supplier losing margin, on the largest single line in the unit.
ideaData.riskNotes: Requires a supplier willing to carry residual risk on a fifteen-year horizon and a reverse logistics route that does not exist yet. Accounting treatment is complex. If the rare earth price collapses, the supplier's residual assumption fails and the contract reprices.
ideaData.validationRequired: Commercial and legal structuring, reverse logistics feasibility, and residual value modelling under rare earth price scenarios.
ideaData.investmentText: Low engineering, high commercial and legal. No tooling.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No automotive benchmark — analogous to aerospace engine service contracts

title: Silicon IGBT module in place of silicon carbide, judged at system level

ideaData.title: Silicon IGBT module in place of silicon carbide, judged at system level
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 104; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Silicon carbide MOSFET six-pack sized for an 800 V bus. Proposal: A Si IGBT six-pack at the same current rating typically costs 40 to 60% less at device level. The honest question is not device cost but system cost: SiC efficiency buys battery capacity, cooling capacity and switching frequency.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: SiC die is roughly 4-6 times the cost per square millimetre of silicon. A Si IGBT six-pack at equal current rating typically lands 40-60% below the SiC module at device level.
ideaData.riskNotes: This is the one idea that must not be judged at part level. On an 800 V bus SiC usually wins back its premium through battery sizing and cooling. Lower switching frequency also grows the DC-link capacitor and can worsen NVH through higher current ripple. Present it as a system trade study, not a saving.
ideaData.validationRequired: System-level energy simulation on the WLTP cycle to quantify the range penalty, then cooling system re-sizing and DC-link re-sizing at the lower switching frequency. Judge the total, not the module.
ideaData.investmentText: Medium. Module qualification and gate driver redesign; cooling and capacitor may both grow.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Nissan Leaf and most pre-2020 400 V BEVs — silicon IGBT traction inverters

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Review-corrected: No part-level saving is booked. The idea's own text says it must be judged at system level and presented as a trade study, and none of the offsetting system costs it names have been quantified by the study: battery capacity to hold range, cooling, a larger DC-link capacitor at lower switching frequency, gate-driver redesign. The device-level delta (40-60% of £181.30 = £72.52-£108.78) is kept only as the gross input to an unbooked system trade note. Public data puts SiC modules at roughly 2-5x the price of an equivalent Si IGBT, which would imply a delta of 50-80%, but those ratios are retail/vendor and older, so the study's own 40-60% is retained. Against it, SiC is reported to cut WLTP/WLTC inverter-related consumption by about 4% (Infineon) to 6% (Rohm). Holding range constant, that consumption rise costs about 4-6% of pack capacity at the BNEF 2025 BEV pack price of USD 99/kWh (£78.21/kWh at 0.79), i.e. £3.13-£4.69 per kWh of pack capacity. The study does not state the pack size, so no single net figure can be computed. The module saving is wiped out by the battery penalty alone for any pack above about 15.5-34.8 kWh, which a 250 kW, 800 V vehicle will almost certainly exceed. Cooling and DC-link growth would make it worse. The study must supply its pack kWh and run the WLTP energy simulation the idea itself demands. 800 V issue: on an 800 V bus a Si solution needs 1200 V IGBTs (e.g. Infineon HybridPACK Drive FS380R12A6T4B, 1200 V/380 A, offered as an 800 V main-inverter kit). 1200 V IGBTs have higher conduction and switching losses than 750 V parts, so the efficiency gap at 800 V is at least as large as the 400 V figures and the 'Nissan Leaf / pre-2020 400 V' benchmark does not transfer. Consider the Si/SiC fusion module (Infineon HybridPACK Drive G2 Fusion, about 30% SiC area claimed to approach full-SiC system efficiency) as the realistic cost-down path.
openQuestions: What is the target vehicle's usable pack kWh and range target? Needed to turn the per-kWh penalty into a net £ figure.
Run the WLTP energy simulation for an 800 V 1200 V-IGBT inverter vs the SiC baseline; the 4-6% figures are vendor/OEM numbers, not this drive unit.
Price the cooling and DC-link capacitor (component #15, £42.00) growth at lower switching frequency.
Evaluate a Si/SiC fusion module as an intermediate option instead of all-Si.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Silicon nitride substrate specified for maximum thermal cycling capability. Proposal: Aluminium nitride or alumina substrates cost materially less than silicon nitride. Alumina is the cheapest but has the lowest conductivity and weakest cycling capability, so the choice follows the real cycling requirement rather than the worst case.

title: Distributed ceramic decoupling alongside a smaller film capacitor

ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 111; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'

ideaData.componentsAffected: DC-link capacitor; EMC filter and Y-capacitors
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Single large film capacitor sized to handle both bulk energy storage and high-frequency ripple. Proposal: Place small ceramic capacitors close to each switch position to absorb the high-frequency ripple, leaving the film capacitor to handle only bulk energy. The film capacitor, which is the expensive element, shrinks.

ideaData.validationRequired: Bus voltage overshoot at maximum load step, ripple current split measurement between film and ceramic, and board flex crack testing.

The automotive isolated delta-sigma modulator AMC1305M25-Q1 is listed at USD 9.7272 each at 1,000+, so 3 x 9.7272 x 0.79 = £23.05. The net is then -£13.25 (a cost increase) before the shunts, the isolated supply on the driver board and the module change, none of which could be priced from public sources. It should not be booked as a saving; the idea's case is accuracy and bandwidth, not cost. reviewCorrection.summary: P17 claimed £38-£67 by charging the saving against the whole £181 power module, but the idea deletes only the £9.80 phase-sensor line and adds shunts and isolated measurement channels. With a published automotive isolated-modulator price the net is a £13.25 cost increase, and the best supplier claim found allows at most £3.27, so the corrected band is -£13.25 to +£3.27. It should not be booked as a saving. The case for it is accuracy, not cost.
reviewCorrection.basis: The mechanism deletes only the three discrete Hall sensors with their mounting and wiring: component #21, £9.80. That is the absolute ceiling. Nothing in the text reduces the £181.30 module, which instead gains integrated shunts. Against the £9.80, three isolated channels are added. The automotive isolated delta-sigma modulator AMC1305M25-Q1 is listed at USD 9.7272 each at 1,000+, so 3 x 9.7272 x 0.79 = £23.05. The net is then -£13.25 (a cost increase) before the shunts, the isolated supply on the driver board and the module change, none of which could be priced from public sources. The best supplier claim found (Riedon) is that an integrated shunt module costs one third less than Hall sensing at 500 A and above; one third of £9.80 is £3.27. TI's own comparison rates shunt and Hall cost as 'Similar'. The corrected band is therefore -£13.25 to +£3.27, centring on roughly zero. It should not be booked as a saving; the idea's case is accuracy and bandwidth, not cost. Distributor coreless Hall prices (Infineon TLE4972 at £1.67-£2.83 each) confirm that the £9.80 baseline line is already lean.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Passive bleed resistors plus a separate active discharge circuit. Proposal: Discharge the DC link by injecting d-axis current into the motor windings under inverter control, using the machine as the dissipating element. Retain only a minimal passive bleed path for the failed-controller case.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Bleed resistors are continuously dissipating components sized for the R100 discharge time. Using the machine as the dissipating element removes most of that hardware.

ideaData.reviewOpenPoints: [CORRECTED 13 Oct 2026] R5 was credited 75-90% of the magnets plus the rotor laminations (£153.75-£184.50), but its own mechanism says only 60-75% of the £171 magnet cost is removed once excitation hardware comes back, and a wound rotor still needs its laminations. The corrected saving is £102.60-£128.25 a unit (£61.56-£76.95 risk-adjusted), consistent with the only published vendor figure (USD 150-200 per vehicle). It must be shown as an alternative to the ten magnet-optimisation ideas, which today double-count the same £171 part (£339.72 claimed against it). ¶ [CRITICAL · quality] Conflict set omits every other magnet idea that was also selected. R5 removes the NdFeB magnets entirely, yet R1 (grain boundary diffusion), R6 (segment count), R13 (rectangular blocks), R16 (resin retention), R19 (dual source/index), M2 (coating), Z5 (shrink machine 'and its magnets'), Z9 (recover magnet value), X2 and Z10 (magnet volume pricing) are all Develop alongside it. Their savings cannot coexist with a magnet-free rotor. Risk-adjusted high savings on the £171.00 magnet part from the Develop list sum to £339.72 for every idea that touches it, or £97.73 for magnet-only ideas plus R5's £110.70. The pack's Rotor group header shows £260.51 of saving against about £269.90 of total rotor part cost. That contradicts the pack's statement that the 77 'do not clash with each other' and Phase 4's statement that 'no two selected ideas can be mutually exclusive'. Evidence: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx '7. Creativity idea register' R5 'Conflicts with' = 'A1, A2, A3, A5, R17, R3, R4, S3'; R1 = 'A4, R12, R2, Z8'; R13/R6 = 'none'; R16 = 'R9, Z19'; R19 = 'Z7, Z8'. '11. Phase 4 evaluation' all = 'Develop'. Pack slide 4: '77 carried forward | These do not clash with each other'; slide 12: 'Rotor | 13 proposals | £260.51 Saving a unit'. Recommendation: Make R5 mutually exclusive with the magnet-optimisation ideas (or present the PM-rotor path and the R5 path as two alternative packages), then re-run the conflict resolution and the group and headline totals before the Director/President review. ¶ [CRITICAL · quality] The saving band does not follow from the idea's own cost mechanism. The mechanism says 'roughly 60-75% of the magnet cost is removed net of the excitation hardware', which is £102.60-£128.25 on the £171.00 magnet. The register instead applies 75-90% to £205.00 (magnets plus rotor lamination stack), giving £153.75-£184.50. A wound rotor still needs a laminated pole stack, so crediting up to 90% of the lamination cost as well is not supported. This is the #1 ranked proposal in the pack (£110.70 a unit). Evidence: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx '7. Creativity idea register' R5: Affected cost 205, Saving % low 0.75, high 0.9, Saving 153.75-184.5; Cost mechanism: 'Roughly 60-75% of the magnet cost is removed net of the excitation hardware that comes back.' Trade-offs: 'Adds a rotor winding, slip rings or a rotating transformer, and an excitation converter.' Recommendation: Ask the study author to reconcile the band with the stated mechanism (60-75% of £171 gives £102.60-£128.25, or about £61.56-£76.95 risk-adjusted at P=0.6) before the deck is shown. ¶ [MINOR · duplicate] True duplicate of an existing Marketplace library idea (same move on the same part). Evidence: Library add150 "Magnet-free externally-excited rotor EDU eliminating rare earth" [extra]; also pt034 "Wound rotor synchronous motor — eliminates rare earth permanent magnets entirely" [legacy-seed]. Recommendation: Link or merge with the library record; keep the study record as the sourced (verbatim) version.

New rotor line, excitation converter development and additional control software', so a £1M NRE looks light and should be challenged; payback = £1,000,000 / (£61.56 x 100,000) = 0.16 years.
reviewCorrection.systemTradeNote: Conflict set. R5 removes the NdFeB magnets entirely, so it is fully mutually exclusive with every idea that only optimises or re-sources those magnets: R1 (grain boundary diffusion), R6 (fewer segments), R13 (rectangular blocks), R19 (dual source and price index), M2 (coating spec), and R16 (cast resin magnet retention: there are no magnets to retain, so the magnet share of its saving vanishes and the end-plate share must be re-assessed for a wound rotor). It partly conflicts with Z5 (second gear ratio to shrink the machine 'and its magnets'), Z9 (end-of-life magnet recovery), X2 and Z10 (volume pricing that includes the magnets). These four must be re-based so that the magnet portion of their saving is removed under the R5 path. Their gear, housing, SiC and bearing portions stay valid. Joint cap: magnet-related claims cannot exceed the £171.00 magnet cost. Selected risk-adjusted high claims touching the magnet line sum to £339.72 (R5 £110.70 + the ten others £229.02), which is 199% of the part. Present two alternative packages. (A) PM-rotor optimisation, magnet-only ideas R1+R6+R13+R19+M2: unrisked £49.59-£116.28 if added, or £44.44-£89.80 when compounded on the shrinking residual magnet cost (each percentage applied to what is left); risk-adjusted high £97.73 added. Either way this is within the £171 cap. Ideas Z5/Z9/X2/Z10/R16 add their magnet share on top, which still must keep the total under £171. (B) Magnet-free R5: £102.60-£128.25 unrisked, £61.56-£76.95 risk-adjusted, with none of the magnet-only ideas allowed alongside it.
openQuestions: No public line-item cost was found for rotor copper winding, slip-ring/brush or rotating-transformer exciter, and field converter; an RFQ or teardown (Munro/A2Mac1 BMW Gen5 rotor) is needed to validate the implied £42.75-£68.40 of returning hardware.

Does the wound rotor at 250 kW / 16,000 rpm need a longer stack or added rotor cooling (Chalmers thesis found an EESM about 87% longer at equal torque in a compressor case)? That would add stator and housing cost not counted here.
Is the £1,000,000 NRE credible for a new rotor line plus an excitation converter and control software (the study's own text rates investment High)?
Re-base Z5, Z9, X2, Z10 and R16 to exclude their magnet share under the R5 package.

evidenceSources.title: EESM can be cost-competitive with or cheaper than a PMSM at high power
evidenceSources.supports: partly: Schaeffler: at higher power the PMSM's larger magnets make it dearer; break-even could be as low as about 120 kW depending on raw-material prices. Brush system and larger design space are the traditional EESM cost drawbacks. A more compact rotor could cut material cost 8-12%.

evidenceSources.title: Active-material cost of a wound-rotor machine is well below that of an IPM
evidenceSources.supports: partly: A literature review reports IPM active-material cost about 2x a comparable wound-rotor design (light EV) and about 3.6x in a truck case. The ratios are for active materials only, excluding excitation hardware (seen via search snippet; full text could not be fetched).

evidenceSources.supports: not found: Several papers and patents state qualitatively that the extra field converter and rotating transformer add size, weight and cost. No USD/EUR line-item price was found for any of them.

title: Reduce magnet segmentation count

ideaData.title: Reduce magnet segmentation count
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 141; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Axially and circumferentially segmented magnets to control eddy losses. Proposal: Cut the number of segments per pole where the rotor eddy loss budget allows. Fewer pieces means less handling, fewer insertion cycles and less adhesive.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Each segment carries handling, placement and adhesive cost. Halving segment count per pole removes roughly half the insertion cycles and adhesive volume on the rotor line.
ideaData.riskNotes: Rotor eddy losses and magnet heating rise, which feeds back into the demagnetisation margin. Interacts directly with R1 and R2 and must be assessed together.
ideaData.validationRequired: Rotor eddy loss measurement and magnet temperature rise at high speed and high frequency, then demagnetisation margin recheck at the elevated temperature.
ideaData.investmentText: Low. Magnet tooling change at the supplier; rotor pocket geometry may need minor revision.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — manufacturing process detail is not publicly attributed to vehicles
ideaData.practiceNote: Standard magnet design lever

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Case carburised and hardened across the whole shaft. Proposal: Induction harden only the bearing journals and seal lands. Cycle time and energy fall sharply, and distortion drops so the post-heat-treat grinding allowance shrinks.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Carburising is a multi-hour furnace cycle for the whole part. Induction hardening is seconds per journal, so energy and cycle time fall by an order of magnitude and distortion drops, cutting grinding stock.
ideaData.riskNotes: Case depth and residual stress profile differ from carburising. Torsional fatigue at the spline root must be re-validated, as must the seal land wear surface.
ideaData.validationRequired: Case depth and hardness profile metallurgy, residual stress measurement, and torsional and bending fatigue test at the spline root and seal land.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Machined aluminium end plates plus separate balance rings. title: Inductive position sensor in place of a variable-reluctance resolver

ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 145; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Wound variable-reluctance resolver with dedicated excitation and demodulation. Proposal: A printed-coil inductive sensor uses a stamped or PCB target and integrates the excitation and demodulation into an ASIC. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Copper windings, the resolver former and the dedicated resolver-to-digital front end on the control board are all removed. The sensor becomes a stamped target plus a PCB coil and an ASIC.
ideaData.riskNotes: EMC susceptibility in a high dv/dt inverter environment is the main risk and needs proving in situ. Accuracy over temperature must be verified against the field-oriented control requirement.
ideaData.validationRequired: Angular accuracy over the full temperature range, EMC immunity measured in situ next to the switching inverter, and functional safety analysis for the position feedback path.
ideaData.investmentText: Medium. Sensor qualification and control board redesign.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — component specification is not disclosed
ideaData.practiceNote: Widely adopted across recent traction drives

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Single-piece annular lamination stamped from strip at roughly 60% utilisation. Proposal: Stamp the core as 12 or 18 segments nested in the strip, lifting utilisation to 85-90%. Segments are joined by interlock and a shrink ring. title: Carry the EDU across multiple programmes to buy volume down

ideaData.componentsAffected: Rotor permanent magnets; Power module (SiC); Gearbox and differential bearings (set); Motor bearings (pair)
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Programme-specific EDU with dedicated part numbers for the major bought components. Proposal: Share the magnet, power module and bearing part numbers across two or three vehicle programmes. Piece price on bought components follows volume tiers, and the major electronic and magnetic components have the steepest tier curves.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Volume tier breaks on power semiconductors and magnets are steep. Doubling annual volume on a part number typically moves 5-12% of its price with no engineering change at all.
ideaData.riskNotes: Requires accepting a compromise specification rather than optimising per application, which usually means carrying some capability that one programme does not need. Cross-programme timing alignment is an organisational problem more than a technical one.
ideaData.validationRequired: No engineering validation beyond confirming the shared specification covers every application's duty. Commercial renegotiation is the work.
ideaData.investmentText: Low engineering, high organisational. No tooling.
ideaData.timeToImplement: 12-24 months, set by programme timing alignment.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: VW MEB platform across ID.3, ID.4, ID.5 and Audi Q4 e-tron — shared EDU across programmes
ideaData.practiceNote: Universal platform strategy across the industry

title: Shorten end-of-line test through parallel testing and reduced burn-in

ideaData.title: Shorten end-of-line test through parallel testing and reduced burn-in
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 169; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.componentsAffected: Control board; Phase current sensors; Resolver / position sensor
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Sequential end-of-line functional test with a conservative burn-in period. Proposal: Test electrical and mechanical characteristics in parallel rather than in sequence, and trim burn-in to the duration that the measured infant mortality curve actually justifies. End-of-line test is often the longest station on the line.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: This is cost of quality, not part cost. Test station cycle time sets line capacity and therefore capital per unit, and end-of-line test is frequently the bottleneck.
ideaData.riskNotes: Reducing burn-in trades directly against field failure rate, and the feedback loop is long. Requires enough production history to characterise infant mortality properly, so it cannot be done at launch.
ideaData.validationRequired: Statistical analysis of field failure data against burn-in duration, and correlation study between the sequential and parallel test methods.
ideaData.investmentText: Medium. Test equipment reconfiguration.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — plant and assembly practice is not vehicle-specific
ideaData.practiceNote: Standard manufacturing optimisation

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Current scrap rates accepted as a process constant rather than a cost target. Proposal: Scrap on a magnet, a power module, a large casting or a ring gear costs the full part value plus the value added before the failure point. title: Reduce the sealed joint count through housing split-line redesign

ideaData.title: Reduce the sealed joint count through housing split-line redesign
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 171; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'
ideaData.studyDecisionReason: Passes the screen, conflicts with nothing already selected, scores at or above 3.00
ideaData.componentsAffected: Main housing; Fasteners and hardware; Static seals and gaskets
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: Housing split lines set by manufacturing convenience, giving four sealed joints. Proposal: Re-place the split lines so that assembly is still possible with two sealed joints rather than four. Every joint deleted removes a sealing face machining operation, a gasket or bead, a fastener set and a leak path.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Each sealed joint carries a machined sealing face, a seal, a fastener set and a leak test risk. Halving the joint count removes all four across two joints.
ideaData.riskNotes: Fewer split lines makes assembly harder and may force a more complex casting or a different assembly sequence. Casting complexity and core count rise, which affects yield.
ideaData.validationRequired: Assembly sequence feasibility study, casting fill and core feasibility, and leak test on the revised joints.
ideaData.investmentText: High. Housing redesign and new tooling.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Reduced sealed-joint housings are inherent to integrated EDUs such as VW APP310 and GM Ultium
ideaData.practiceNote: Standard integrated housing practice

title: Decompose the ASIL rating to relax hardware on the lower-rated paths

ideaData.title: Decompose the ASIL rating to relax hardware on the lower-rated paths
ideaData.sourcePointer: EDU_Function_Analysis.xlsx › '7. Creativity idea register' row 172; '11. Phase 4 evaluation'

ideaData.targetFunctions: Control Torque; Detect Fault; Communicate Data
ideaData.componentsAffected: Control board; Gate driver board; Conformal coating and potting
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: A single high ASIL rating applied uniformly across the control hardware. Proposal: ASIL decomposition allocates the safety requirement across redundant paths, so not every element needs the highest rating. Lower-rated paths can use cheaper components with less diagnostic coverage.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Automotive components carry a substantial premium for higher ASIL ratings and the diagnostic coverage that goes with them. Applying the rating only where it is genuinely required removes that premium from the rest.
ideaData.riskNotes: Decomposition must be argued rigorously and independence between the decomposed paths proven, or the argument collapses at assessment. Getting this wrong is a safety exposure, not a cost exposure.
ideaData.validationRequired: Full ISO 26262 decomposition argument with independence analysis, reviewed by an independent assessor.
ideaData.investmentText: Medium to high. Functional safety engineering effort.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: No public benchmark — control and software strategy is not disclosed
ideaData.practiceNote: Standard functional safety practice
